Consult Summary:
- 53-year-old man with one week of a non-painful, slightly warm swelling over the left elbow, clinically assessed as probable olecranon bursitis; started on oral NSAID and blood tests arranged with planned follow-up.

History:
- Presenting complaint:
  - Noticed swelling of the left elbow approximately one week ago while showering.
  - Swelling described as non-painful overall, slightly warm, with a sensation of fluid/“weird” fullness at the site.
  - Can move the elbow normally; no reported loss of range of motion.
- Timeline/progression:
  - Onset: ~1 week prior to consultation.
  - Course: patient states it “feels a bit better now.”
- Exacerbating/relieving factors:
  - No reported recent trauma or injury to the elbow.
  - No specific aggravating activities reported; patient is sedentary at work (desk job) and runs 2–3 times per week.
- Associated symptoms/review of systems:
  - No fever reported.
  - No widespread joint swelling reported; patient has a history of intermittent joint pain related to diagnosed osteoarthritis.
  - No skin rash or history of eczema.
  - No redness or spreading erythema at the time of exam beyond slight warmth; no severe pain suggestive of septic arthritis.
- Pertinent negatives:
  - Denies systemic symptoms (fever/chills).
  - Denies prior episodes of similar elbow swelling.
  - Denies known family history of rheumatoid arthritis or lupus (patient uncertain about broader family rheumatologic history).

Past Medical History:
- Osteoarthritis — diagnosed by GP several years ago; intermittent joint pain reported.
- Allergies: peanut allergy (food allergy).
- No other chronic medical conditions reported.
- Medications: patient states no regular medications.

Social History:
- Occupation: desk-based job (not physically demanding).
- Exercise: runs 2–3 times per week.
- Smoking/alcohol/substance use: not documented in the transcript.
- No financial or other lifestyle concerns documented.

Family History:
- Patient uncertain; explicitly denies known family history of rheumatoid arthritis or lupus when asked, but overall family rheumatologic history is unclear per patient statement.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: not documented.
- Inspection of left elbow:
  - Visible swelling at the tip/olecranon region of the left elbow.
  - Overlying skin slightly warm compared to adjacent skin.
  - Skin over tip noted as somewhat dry.
- Palpation:
  - Tip of the elbow not markedly tender to direct pressure; area adjacent to the swelling described by patient as feeling “weird” and mildly uncomfortable on pressure.
- Range of motion:
  - Patient able to move elbow normally; full mobility reported/observed.
- Other exam findings: none documented.

Investigations:
- No investigations performed during the visit.
- Plan to perform blood tests: full screen including inflammatory markers, infection markers, rheumatologic antibodies, and assessment for gout.
- Blood test forms to be mailed to patient with instructions on where to attend for phlebotomy.
- Anticipated result timeframe communicated: approximately 5–6 days after sample; timing may vary depending on form delivery and test completion.

Assessment & Plan:
- Issue 1: Left elbow swelling — probable olecranon bursitis
  - Assessment: Clinical impression is bursitis (inflammation of bursal sac) at the olecranon; current appearance not suggestive of septic arthritis.
  - Plan:
    - Start ibuprofen 400 mg twice daily; take after food; stop if develops heartburn (dose and frequency documented; route not explicitly documented).
    - Arrange blood tests as above (inflammatory markers, infection screen, rheumatologic antibodies, gout screen).
    - Arrange follow-up appointment after blood test results; follow-up may be video/phone or face-to-face per patient preference.
    - Advise urgent reassessment (phone/video or in-person) if the elbow becomes very red, very painful, or if redness spreads — these features would warrant emergency assessment for possible septic arthritis.
- Issue 2: Osteoarthritis (past diagnosis)
  - Assessment: Known history diagnosed by GP several years ago; intermittent joint pain.
  - Plan:
    - No acute change to osteoarthritis management documented in this visit.
    - Continue usual activities as tolerated; no additional treatments specified beyond NSAID for current bursitis.
- Issue 3: Peanut allergy
  - Assessment: Patient reports peanut allergy.
  - Plan:
    - No changes documented; counsel to avoid peanuts as per usual precautions.

General plan items:
- Send blood test forms to patient’s home with instructions for sample collection.
- Expect blood test results in approximately 5–6 days after testing; clinician will review results and follow up with patient.
- Patient to schedule or accept follow-up (phone/video or face-to-face) after blood tests; instructed to seek earlier in-person review if symptoms worsen acutely.
- Provide patient education about signs of septic arthritis and when to seek urgent care.

Quality checks (document_quality):
- Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - Vital signs (temperature, pulse, blood pressure) not recorded.
  - No imaging performed or ordered (e.g., ultrasound or x-ray) though sometimes considered for bursitis/gout — not documented in transcript.
  - Medication route for ibuprofen not explicitly documented (dose and frequency documented).
  - No formal medication reconciliation beyond patient report of no regular medications.
  - No laboratory results available at time of consult.
- Internal conflicts from transcript:
  - Patient initially denied family rheumatologic disease but was uncertain about family history overall; family history remains unclear (conflict/uncertainty noted).
  - No other direct contradictions identified.
- Transcript quality:
  - Audio/transcript understandable with minor conversational interruptions; clinical details are clear and adequately documented.
